why.support: New workers are keen and in a hurry. That's when people get hurt. Safety signs and steps are texts that keep you safe. Read them fast and right.
why.core: Young workers are new, keen and often in a hurry — and that's when people get hurt. Safety signs and procedures are texts written to keep you in one piece. Reading them fast and right is a real-life skill.
why.extend: New workers are injured at higher rates than experienced ones, often because nobody explained the risks or they didn't feel able to ask. Safety signs and procedures are carefully designed texts: their colours, symbols, order and wording all do a job.

articles.title: Signs and steps that keep you safe

body.support:
Workplaces have **signs** and **steps** to keep you safe.

**Signs** use colours and shapes:

- **Red circle with a line**: not allowed.
- **Blue circle**: you **must** do it.
- **Yellow triangle**: **danger** nearby.
- **Green**: first aid and exits.

A **procedure** is a list of safe steps. It has a title. It tells you what gear to wear. Then it has numbered steps.

The steps use order words: *first*, *then*, *after*. They use **if** words too: *If the oil spits, step back.*

The big rule: **if you're not sure, ask.**
body.core:
Workplaces use two kinds of safety text: **signs** and **procedures**.

**Signs** are built to be read in a second, so they use colour and shape:

- **Red circle with a line**: not allowed (*No smoking*).
- **Blue circle**: you **must** do this (*Wear ear protection*).
- **Yellow triangle**: **warning**, there's a hazard nearby (*Hot surface*).
- **Green**: safety and emergency (*First aid*, *Exit*).

A **procedure** tells you how to do a job safely. Most follow the same stages: a **title**, the **PPE** you need, the **hazards**, then numbered **steps**.

The steps use **order words** like *first*, *then*, *before* and *after*, so you know the sequence. They also use **if** words: *If the oil spits, step back.* Those are the steps that save fingers.

And the most important rule isn't on any sign: **if you're not sure, ask.** You have the right to be trained and supervised.
body.extend:
Workplaces rely on two kinds of safety text: **signs** and **procedures**.

**Signs** are designed to be understood in a glance, so they use a standard code of colour and shape:

- **Red circle with a diagonal line**: prohibited (*No smoking*).
- **Blue circle**: mandatory (*Wear ear protection*).
- **Yellow triangle**: warning, a hazard is present (*Hot surface*).
- **Green**: safe conditions and emergency information (*First aid*, *Exit*).

A **safe work procedure** is organised into predictable stages: title, PPE, hazards, then numbered steps. Its language is precise and cohesive. Time connectives (*first*, *before*, *once*) set the sequence, and conditional connectives (*if*, *unless*, *when*) mark the moments where you must stop or change what you're doing.

None of this works if workers feel unable to speak up. Under Victorian law, employers must provide training and supervision, and you are entitled to ask.

caseStudies.title: Two injuries in one day

body.support:
In 2022, **WorkSafe Victoria** told the story of a **16-year-old apprentice**.

On a building site, he was hurt **two times in one day**. Another worker fired a **nail gun**. The nail went into the apprentice's head. He was in hospital for a week.

The company did not report it. It even **hid the nail guns** from the safety inspectors.

A court fined the company **$130,000**.

Young workers must be trained and watched over. And they have the right to speak up.
body.core:
In December 2022, **WorkSafe Victoria** reported a court case about a **16-year-old apprentice carpenter**.

On a building site in Glen Waverley, the apprentice was hurt **twice in one day**. In the second incident, he and a more experienced worker were at opposite ends of a doorframe. The other worker fired a **nail gun**. The nail went into the apprentice's forehead and through his skull. He spent a week in hospital.

The company didn't report either injury, which the law says it must. It was found guilty of **eight charges**. These included not having a safe way of working, and **hiding the nail guns** from inspectors. It was fined **$130,000**.

WorkSafe's message: young workers need training, supervision and a safe system of work — and they have the right to speak up.
body.extend:
In December 2022, **WorkSafe Victoria** reported the result of a court case about a **16-year-old apprentice carpenter**.

On a Glen Waverley building site, the apprentice was injured **twice in one day**. In the second incident, he and a more experienced worker were at opposite ends of a doorframe. The other worker fired a **nail gun**. The nail went into the apprentice's forehead and through his skull. He spent a week in hospital.

Neither incident was reported to WorkSafe, as the law requires. The company was convicted on **eight charges**. They included failing to provide a safe system of work, and getting in the way of the inquiry by **hiding the nail guns** from inspectors. It was fined **$130,000**.

The case shows why procedures, supervision and reporting exist. Each one could have stopped an injury.

teacher.overview: Students read safety signs (colour and shape as visual language) and safe work procedures (staged procedural texts that use time and conditional connectives), then write their own procedure with a sign. The case study is a WorkSafe Victoria prosecution after a 16-year-old apprentice was injured twice in one day.
prep: Print workbooks (colour printing helps for signs, or have coloured pencils).
Optional: photograph real signs around the school (science lab, canteen, workshop).
Optional: invite a VET, trades or canteen staff member to show a real procedure.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Signs
steps: **Hook (10 min):** sign walk around the school, or a slideshow of real signs. What does each one want?

steps: **Annotate (15 min):** the fryer procedure; model stages and connectives.
**Join it up (10 min):** rewrite vague steps.

**Exit (5 min):** one thing you'd say if asked to do something unsafe.

steps: **Check & reflect (15 min):** quick check, reflection, request sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Signs:** goggles (blue) — must; phone with line (red) — must not; flame (yellow) — warning; white cross (green) — first aid; lightning (yellow) — warning (electrical); ear muffs (blue) — must.

**Procedure:** 1 PPE; 2 hazards; 3 order word “first” with an exact time; 4 order word “before”; 5 conditional “if” step; 6 report back.

**Join it up (samples):** If the toaster is stuck, first unplug it. / If the ladder is wobbly, don't climb it — tell your supervisor. / If there's a spill, first put out a wet-floor sign, then mop it up.

WorkSafe Victoria — Plumber fined after driving ute with teen in toolbox (2024)

realityCheck: **The case study is confronting.** A nail through a 16-year-old's skull will hit hard, especially for students who work on sites or have family who've been hurt. Read it as a class, keep the focus on what should have happened, and give a heads-up beforehand.
**Students with jobs are your experts.** Many 14–17 year olds work in fast food, retail or on farms. Let them name real hazards; it makes the writing task authentic.
**Colour matters.** Sign meaning depends on colour. Black-and-white printing makes the sort harder, so use colour, coloured pencils or the app.
**Speaking up is the real outcome.** The “What would you say?” question is worth discussing aloud: many young workers don't feel they can say no.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's practical, local and low-tech. The final mission doubles as useful work-experience prep.
